title: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates
short: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates
lead: Solids with an axis of symmetry or a center of symmetry are described most simply in cylindrical or spherical coordinates. This section changes triple integrals to cylindrical and spherical coordinates, finds the volume element of each, and uses them for cones, spheres, paraboloids, an ellipsoid and the spaces of l’Hemisfèric and a hot air balloon.
objectives: Evaluate a triple integral by changing to cylindrical coordinates.
Evaluate a triple integral by changing to spherical coordinates.
summary_html:
• To evaluate a triple integral in cylindrical coordinates, use the iterated integral $$\int_{\ktheta =\alpha}^{\ktheta =\beta } \;\int_{r=g_{1}(\ktheta )}^{r=g_{2}(\ktheta )} \;\int_{z=\kufn_{1}(r,\ktheta )}^{z=\kufn_{2}(r,\ktheta )} \kf(r,\ktheta ,z) r\;dz\;dr\;d\theta .$$
  • To evaluate a triple integral in spherical coordinates, use the iterated integral $$\int_{\ktheta =\alpha}^{\ktheta =\beta } \;\int_{\rho =g_{1}(\ktheta )}^{\rho =g_{2}(\ktheta )} \;\int_{\kphi =\kufn_{1}(r,\ktheta )}^{\kphi =\kufn_{2}(r,\ktheta )} \kf(\rho ,\ktheta ,\kphi ) {\rho }^{2}\sin \kphi \;d\varphi \;d\rho \;d\theta .$$

$f(x,y,z)=e^{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}},$ $B=\{(x,y,z)|1\le x^{2}+y^{2}\le 4,y\le 0,x\le y\sqrt{3},2\le z\le 3\}$

In the following exercises, evaluate the triple integrals $\iiint\limits_{B}f(x,y,z)dV$ over the solid $B.$

a. Let $B$ be a cylindrical shell with inner radius $a,$ outer radius $b,$ and height $c,$ where $0\lt a\lt b$ and $c\gt 0.$ Assume that a function $F$ defined on $B$ can be expressed in cylindrical coordinates as $F(x,y,z)=f(r)+h(z),$ where $f$ and $h$ are differentiable functions. If $\int_a^{b} \tilde{f}(r)dr=0$ and $\tilde{h}(0)=0,$ where $\tilde{f}$ and $\tilde{h}$ are antiderivatives of $f$ and $h,$ respectively, show that

$$\iiint\limits_{B}F(x,y,z)dV =2\pi c(b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a))+\pi (b^{2}-a^{2})\tilde{h}(c).$$

b. Use the previous result to show that $\iiint\limits_{B}(z+\sin \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}) dx\;dy\;dz=6{\pi}^{2}(\pi -2),$ where $B$ is a cylindrical shell with inner radius $\pi ,$ outer radius $2\pi ,$ and height $2.$

answer.solution:
a. In cylindrical coordinates $B$ is $a\le r\le b,$ $0\le\theta\le 2\pi,$ $0\le z\le c,$ and $dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz,$ so $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=2\pi c\int_{a}^{b}rf(r)\,dr+2\pi\cdot\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{2}\int_{0}^{c}h(z)\,dz.$ By parts, $\int_{a}^{b}rf(r)\,dr=[r\tilde{f}(r)]_{a}^{b}-\int_{a}^{b}\tilde{f}(r)\,dr=b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a),$ since $\int_{a}^{b}\tilde{f}\,dr=0;$ and $\int_{0}^{c}h\,dz=\tilde{h}(c)-\tilde{h}(0)=\tilde{h}(c).$ Together, $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=2\pi c(b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a))+\pi (b^{2}-a^{2})\tilde{h}(c).$

b. Here $F=\sin r+z,$ so $f(r)=\sin r$ with $\tilde{f}(r)=-\cos r,$ whose integral over $[\pi,2\pi]$ is $-[\sin r]_{\pi}^{2\pi}=0,$ and $h(z)=z$ with $\tilde{h}(z)=\frac{z^{2}}{2},$ $\tilde{h}(0)=0.$ With $a=\pi,$ $b=2\pi,$ $c=2:$ $b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a)=-2\pi-\pi=-3\pi,$ so the integral is $2\pi(2)(-3\pi)+\pi(4\pi^{2}-\pi^{2})(2)=-12\pi^{2}+6\pi^{3}=6\pi^{2}(\pi-2).$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, evaluate the triple integrals $\iiint\limits_{B}f(x,y,z)dV$ over the solid $B.$

a. Let $B$ be a cylindrical shell with inner radius $a,$ outer radius $b,$ and height $c,$ where $0\lt a\lt b$ and $c\gt 0.$ Assume that a function $F$ defined on $B$ can be expressed in cylindrical coordinates as $F(x,y,z)=f(r)g(\theta )h(z),$ where $f,g,\;\text{and}\;h$ are differentiable functions. If $\int_a^{b} \tilde{f}(r)dr=0 ,$ where $\tilde{f}$ is an antiderivative of $f,$ show that

$$\iiint\limits_{B}F(x,y,z)dV =[b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a)]\;[\tilde{g}(2\pi )-\tilde{g}(0)]\;[\tilde{h}(c)-\tilde{h}(0)],$$

where $\tilde{g}$ and $\tilde{h}$ are antiderivatives of $g$ and $h,$ respectively.

b. Use the previous result to show that $\iiint\limits_{B}z\;\sin \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} dx\;dy\;dz=-12{\pi}^{2},$ where $B$ is a cylindrical shell with inner radius $\pi ,$ outer radius $2\pi ,$ and height $2.$

answer.solution:
a. Over the cylindrical shell $a\le r\le b,$ $0\le\theta\le 2\pi,$ $0\le z\le c$ the integrand $f(r)g(\theta)h(z)\,r$ is a product of functions of one variable each, so $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=(\int_{a}^{b}rf(r)\,dr)(\int_{0}^{2\pi}g(\theta)\,d\theta)(\int_{0}^{c}h(z)\,dz).$ As in the preceding exercise, integration by parts and $\int_{a}^{b}\tilde{f}\,dr=0$ give $\int_{a}^{b}rf(r)\,dr=b\tilde{f}(b)-a\tilde{f}(a),$ and the other two factors are $\tilde{g}(2\pi)-\tilde{g}(0)$ and $\tilde{h}(c)-\tilde{h}(0).$

b. For $z\sin r,$ take $f=\sin r$ ($\tilde{f}=-\cos r,$ with zero integral over $[\pi,2\pi]$), $g=1$ ($\tilde{g}=\theta$) and $h=z$ ($\tilde{h}=\frac{z^{2}}{2}$): the integral is $(-3\pi)(2\pi)(2)=-12\pi^{2}.$

In the following exercises, evaluate the triple integral $\iiint\limits_{B}f(x,y,z)dV$ over the solid $B.$

$f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}},$ $B$ is bounded above by the half-sphere $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=9$ with $z\ge 0$ and below by the cone $z^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}.$

Show that if $F(\rho ,\theta ,\varphi )=f(\rho )g(\theta )h(\varphi )$ is a continuous function on the spherical box $B=\{(\rho ,\theta ,\varphi )|a\le \rho \le b,\alpha \le \theta \le \beta ,\gamma \le \varphi \le \psi \},$ then

$$\iiint\limits_{B}F\;dV =(\int_a^{b} {\rho }^{2}f(\rho )dr )(\int_{\alpha}^{\beta } g(\theta )d\theta )(\int_{\gamma }^{\psi } h(\varphi )\sin \varphi \;d\varphi ).$$

answer.solution: In spherical coordinates $dV=\rho^{2}\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\varphi,$ so over the spherical box $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=\int_{\gamma}^{\psi}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b}f(\rho)g(\theta)h(\varphi)\rho^{2}\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\theta\,d\varphi.$ The integrand is the product of $\rho^{2}f(\rho),$ $g(\theta)$ and $h(\varphi)\sin\varphi,$ each a function of one variable, and the limits are constants, so the iterated integral is the product $(\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f(\rho)\,d\rho)(\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}g(\theta)\,d\theta)(\int_{\gamma}^{\psi}h(\varphi)\sin\varphi\,d\varphi).$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, evaluate the triple integral $\iiint\limits_{B}f(x,y,z)dV$ over the solid $B.$

a. A function $F$ is said to have spherical symmetry if it depends on the distance to the origin only, that is, it can be expressed in spherical coordinates as $F(x,y,z)=f(\rho ),$ where $\rho =\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}.$ Show that

$$\iiint\limits_{B}F(x,y,z)dV =2\pi \int_a^{b} {\rho }^{2}f(\rho )d\rho ,$$

where $B$ is the region between the upper concentric hemispheres of radii $a$ and $b$ centered at the origin, with $0\lt a\lt b$ and $F$ a spherical function defined on $B.$

b. Use the previous result to show that $\iiint\limits_{B}(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2})\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}\;dV =21\pi ,$ where

$$B=\{(x,y,z)|1\le x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\le 2,z\ge 0\}.$$

answer.solution:
a. The region between the upper hemispheres is $a\le\rho\le b,$ $0\le\theta\le 2\pi,$ $0\le\varphi\le\frac{\pi}{2}.$ By the preceding exercise with $g=h=1,$ $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=(\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f(\rho)\,d\rho)(2\pi)(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin\varphi\,d\varphi)=2\pi\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f(\rho)\,d\rho.$

b. Here $F=\rho^{2}\cdot\rho=\rho^{3},$ so the integral is $2\pi\int\rho^{5}\,d\rho.$ For the region printed, $1\le\rho\le\sqrt{2},$ this is $2\pi\cdot\frac{8-1}{6}=\frac{7\pi}{3};$ the value $21\pi$ is the integral between the hemispheres of radii $1$ and $2,$ $2\pi\cdot\frac{64-1}{6}=21\pi.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, evaluate the triple integral $\iiint\limits_{B}f(x,y,z)dV$ over the solid $B.$

a. Let $B$ be the region between the upper concentric hemispheres of radii a and b centered at the origin and situated in the first octant, where $0\lt a\lt b.$ Consider F a function defined on B whose form in spherical coordinates $(\rho ,\theta ,\varphi )$ is $F(x,y,z)=f(\rho )\cos \varphi .$ Show that if $g(a)=g(b)=0$ and $\int_a^{b} h(\rho )d\rho =0 ,$ then

$$\iiint\limits_{B}F(x,y,z)dV =\frac{{\pi}^{2}}{4}[ah(a)-bh(b)],$$

where $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$ and $h$ is an antiderivative of $g.$

b. Use the previous result to show that $\iiint\limits_{B}\frac{z\;\cos \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}}dV =\frac{3{\pi}^{2}}{2},$ where $B$ is the region between the upper concentric hemispheres of radii $\pi$ and $2\pi$ centered at the origin and situated in the first octant.

answer.solution:
a. In the first octant between the hemispheres, $a\le\rho\le b,$ $0\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2},$ $0\le\varphi\le\frac{\pi}{2},$ so $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=(\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f(\rho)\,d\rho)(\frac{\pi}{2})(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos\varphi\sin\varphi\,d\varphi)=\frac{\pi}{4}\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f(\rho)\,d\rho.$ Integrating by parts twice with $g^{\prime}=f,$ $h^{\prime}=g,$ $g(a)=g(b)=0$ and $\int_{a}^{b}h\,d\rho=0:$ $\int_{a}^{b}\rho^{2}f\,d\rho=[\rho^{2}g]_{a}^{b}-2\int_{a}^{b}\rho g\,d\rho=-2([\rho h]_{a}^{b}-\int_{a}^{b}h\,d\rho)=2[ah(a)-bh(b)].$ Hence $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=\frac{\pi}{2}[ah(a)-bh(b)].$

b. $\frac{z\cos\rho}{\rho}=\cos\varphi\cos\rho,$ so $f=\cos\rho,$ $g=\sin\rho$ (zero at $\pi$ and $2\pi$) and $h=-\cos\rho$ (with $\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}h\,d\rho=0$). Then $ah(a)-bh(b)=\pi(1)-2\pi(-1)=3\pi,$ and the integral is $\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot 3\pi=\frac{3\pi^{2}}{2}.$

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The integral $\int_0^{2\pi} \;\int_0^{1} \;\int_r^{1} dz\;dr\;d\theta$ represents the volume of a right cone.

answer.solution: False. The region $0\le\theta\le 2\pi,$ $0\le r\le 1,$ $r\le z\le 1$ is the right cone with vertex at the origin, radius $1$ and height $1,$ but in cylindrical coordinates $dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta,$ and the integrand here lacks the factor $r.$ The integral as written is $\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(1-r)\,dr\,d\theta=\pi,$ while the cone’s volume is $\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}\int_{r}^{1}r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\int_{0}^{1}(r-r^{2})\,dr=\frac{\pi}{3}.$

footnotes.html: In the first integral the upper limit of $r$ is printed $\sqrt{4-r^{2}};$ on the sphere $r^{2}+z^{2}=4$ it is $r=\sqrt{4-z^{2}},$ as in $E_{1}$ above.
The first order is $d\rho\;d\varphi\;d\theta,$ printed $d\rho\;d\theta\;d\theta,$ as part a’s integral shows.

The integrand is $\rho^{2}\sin\varphi,$ printed $\rho^{2}\sin\theta,$ and in the second line $\varphi$ and $\theta$ trade places; since both run over $[0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ the value $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$ is unchanged.

The change of coordinates is $x=a\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,$ $y=b\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,$ $z=c\rho\cos\varphi,$ and the integrand that follows is $abc\,\rho^{2}\sin\varphi;$ as printed, with $\theta$ and $\varphi$ traded, the value $\frac{4}{3}\pi abc$ is the same.
The region is $\{(r,\theta,z)\mid 0\le\theta\le 2\pi,\;0\le r\le 1,\;r\le z\le 2-r^{2}\},$ as the integral’s limits show; it is printed with $0\le z\le 1,$ $z\le r\le 2-z^{2}.$

The region is bounded below by the $r\theta$-plane, so $z$ runs from $0,$ not from $r:$ $\{(r,\theta,z)\mid 0\le\theta\le 2\pi,\;0\le r\le 1,\;0\le z\le\sqrt{4-r^{2}}\}$ and $V=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{4-r^{2}}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}r\,d\theta\,dz\,dr.$
The first factor’s variable is printed $dr;$ it is $d\rho.$
With $B$ as printed, $1\le\rho\le\sqrt{2},$ the integral is $\frac{7\pi}{3};$ the value $21\pi$ belongs to the region $1\le x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\le 4,$ between the hemispheres of radii $1$ and $2.$
The factor in part a works out to $\frac{\pi}{2},$ not $\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}:$ $\iiint_{B}F\,dV=\frac{\pi}{2}[ah(a)-bh(b)],$ which gives part b’s $\frac{3\pi^{2}}{2}.$
